<reason>Side A wins by narrowing the motion to faithful dubbing of an already-performed script, distinguishing it from open-ended cloning, new dialogue, and reuse for unrelated projects that can be expressly banned. B repeatedly relied on those broader abuses without proving they are inherent to dubbing. A also turned B's answers into a damaging fork: opt-in is either just a clearer upfront clause or a refusable/revocable gate whose admitted consequence is replacing performers or skipping territories, harming lesser-known actors and audiences most.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 answers B's questions directly, concedes permanent replicas for new dialogue are not licensed, then uses B's own replacement-or-skip-territory answer to show opt-in produces the displacement and access losses B claimed to prevent.</best_rebuttal>
